prompt.en: Party T won 3 Lok Sabha seats, all from one State, which is allotted 80 seats, and polled 4% of the valid votes in four States. It is not a recognised State party anywhere. In four sentences, explain why each of the three national routes fails, and say what Party T can still do.

label.en: The first route fails because Party T polled less than 6% of the valid votes in the four States and won fewer than four Lok Sabha seats.

level1.en: What two things does the first national route ask for?

clue.en: The first route asks for not less than 6% of valid votes in four or more States, and four Lok Sabha seats as well.

level2Template.en: The first route fails because 4% is below ___ of the valid votes.

label.en: The second route fails because 3 seats are far below 2% of the 543 Lok Sabha seats, and all of them come from one State.

level1.en: How many seats is 2% of 543, and from how many States must they come?

clue.en: 2% of 543 is about 11 seats, and the candidates must be elected from at least three States.

level2Template.en: The second route fails because Party T needs about ___ seats from at least three States.

label.en: The third route fails because Party T is not recognised as a State party in any State, and the route needs four.

level1.en: What does the third route ask a party to be already?

clue.en: The third route asks for recognition as a State party in at least four States.

level2Template.en: The third route fails because Party T is a recognised State party in ___ State.

label.en: Party T remains a registered party and its candidates can still contest, but it is not allotted a reserved symbol.

level1.en: Does failing to be recognised stop a party's candidates from contesting?

clue.en: Registered unrecognised parties can contest. Only national and State parties are allotted election symbols.

level2Template.en: Party T remains registered and can still ___ elections, without a reserved symbol.

text.en: The first national route fails, because Party T polled only 4% of the valid votes where 6% is needed, and it won 3 Lok Sabha seats where four are needed.
The second route fails, because 2% of the 543 Lok Sabha seats is about 11 seats and Party T won 3, all from one State rather than three.
The third route fails, because Party T is not recognised as a State party in any State and the route requires four.
Party T therefore remains a registered party. Its candidates can still contest elections, but it is not allotted a reserved symbol.

explanation.en: Each route fails on its own figure: 4% is below 6% with too few seats; 3 seats is below about 11; and no State record stands against the four needed. Party T stays registered, and its candidates can still contest.

hints.en: Take the three national routes one at a time and write the figure each one needs.
